title: NAACP, Urban League and white guilt; Hinton's thanks
summary: Maxwell thought white-run civil rights groups were guilt-driven; Hinton praises his kindness, including to Ozie Johnson.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: The point that I'm trying to make is not that I was angry, and not because I was trying to fight a cause, it's just because it was my friends that they were hassling with, you know. I belong to the organizations like NAACP and Urban League and those things but I never thought too much of them, mainly because they were run by white people. And I didn't think anything would really happen until black people took over those organizations.

But in those days, you know, it was a white people's organization, they worked off their guilty conscience, whatever it was. They'd give money and sit down and have a cup of coffee with their maid and feel virtuous, you know.

I know you've always been so very liberal and kind and so helpful along all those causes. And your friends, I know you've had so many guys -- black friends, for example, I consider myself one, surely. And I can never forget your kindness to the late Ozie Johnson when he was ill. I remember one time you just called me off on the side and gave me $100.00 and said, would you please see Ozie gets this. I shall never forget all those kinds things you've done. And that has been consistent with your life.
